variants.title: Trace the multimodal request
variants.context: A multimodal request crosses four boundaries: admit and normalize the media, encode each modality while recording every transformation, align related evidence without erasing its provenance, then validate and release. Model inference is one stage inside that path, not the path itself.
variants.prompt: An invoice image arrives with a purchase order reference and must be validated before payment. Put the boundaries in order.

items.text: Bind the extracted total to the purchase order record while keeping both values and their sources distinct.
Run OCR on the page and record crop coordinates and the preprocessing version alongside the extracted text.
Apply the schema, deterministic business rules, and approval policy before any payment is authorized.
Validate type, size, tenant policy, consent, and malware status before any expensive processing.

variants.hint: Which boundary is the last place a generated value can still be stopped?
variants.explanation: Admission protects the system before work begins, and the action boundary keeps generated proposals separate from authorized state changes.

variants.title: Trace the multimodal request
variants.context: A multimodal request crosses four boundaries: admit and normalize the media, encode each modality while recording every transformation, align related evidence without erasing its provenance, then validate and release. Model inference is one stage inside that path, not the path itself.
variants.prompt: A recorded meeting must produce a summary with owners and decisions. Put the boundaries in order.

items.text: Transcribe the audio into timestamped segments and keep the segment identifiers with the text.
Relate the agenda items to the transcript spans without merging them into one undifferentiated note.
Check duration, tenant policy, and retention class for the uploaded recording.
Apply the output schema and confidence gates, then mark decisions that lack a supporting transcript span.

variants.hint: Provenance is created during encoding and spent during release.
variants.explanation: Transcription is a transformation, so its segments and versions must be recorded before alignment can bind a decision to the words that produced it.

variants.title: Trace the multimodal request
variants.context: A multimodal request crosses four boundaries: admit and normalize the media, encode each modality while recording every transformation, align related evidence without erasing its provenance, then validate and release. Model inference is one stage inside that path, not the path itself.
variants.prompt: A support screenshot contains a visible API key. Put the boundaries in order, ending with the release decision.

items.text: Extract the on screen text and record the region coordinates for every extracted span.
Redact the credential span, disclose that visual verification was limited, and release the reply.
Join the extracted error text to the conversation history while keeping the two sources separable.
Accept the screenshot under the support task identifier and its retention class.

variants.hint: Redaction is a release decision, not an encoding accident.
variants.explanation: Derived text, crops, and thumbnails inherit the source data classification, so the release boundary owns redaction and disclosure.

variants.title: Work the timeline
variants.context: Audio and video are timelines, so coverage depends on when the system observes. Segment the media by time, select the evidence the question needs, align streams by timestamp while keeping source identifiers, then report which intervals were observed, skipped, or corrupt.
variants.prompt: A safety inspection video must be reviewed for hazards. Put the timeline steps in order.

items.text: Sample around motion and domain events, keeping the frames before and after each candidate hazard.
Return the interval map showing which segments were observed, skipped, or unreadable.
Decode the recording into scene boundaries and timestamped windows.
Relate the sampled frames to sensor metadata by timestamp while retaining the original source identifiers.

variants.hint: Which step decides what the answer is allowed to claim about the unwatched parts?
variants.explanation: Event aware sampling protects short actions, and the coverage report stops the answer from implying that the whole recording was reviewed.

variants.title: Work the timeline
variants.context: Audio and video are timelines, so coverage depends on when the system observes. Segment the media by time, select the evidence the question needs, align streams by timestamp while keeping source identifiers, then report which intervals were observed, skipped, or corrupt.
variants.prompt: A one hour meeting recording must be summarized with slides and speaker turns. Put the timeline steps in order.

items.text: State which minutes had no usable audio so the summary does not imply full attendance coverage.
Split the recording into speech windows and slide change boundaries.
Choose evenly spaced coverage because the task is a broad summary rather than event detection.
Align transcript segments, slide frames, and the agenda by timestamp.

variants.hint: The sampling policy follows the question being asked.
variants.explanation: A broad summary tolerates uniform sampling, while the coverage report still has to expose the intervals that produced nothing.

variants.title: Work the timeline
variants.context: Audio and video are timelines, so coverage depends on when the system observes. Segment the media by time, select the evidence the question needs, align streams by timestamp while keeping source identifiers, then report which intervals were observed, skipped, or corrupt.
variants.prompt: A compliance review finds a corrupt segment in the middle of the recording. Put the steps in order, ending with the escalation.

items.text: Select the intervals the compliance question requires rather than sampling for cost.
Route the gap to human review and keep the interval map with the case record.
Discover during alignment that one interval decodes to nothing usable.
Segment the recording into auditable intervals with start and end timestamps.

variants.hint: A compliance answer is only as strong as its interval map.
variants.explanation: Gaps and corrupt segments are routed to review instead of being silently skipped, because a missing interval is evidence about the answer's limits.

variants.title: Budget the route
variants.context: The routing lab models a request as the task base latency plus the slowest admitted modality encoder plus the fusion overhead. Encoders run in parallel, so admitting a second cheap modality does not add its latency, and each fusion pattern carries its own overhead.
variants.prompt: The invoice task has a base latency of 180 ms. It admits text at 35 ms and image evidence at 310 ms, and it uses evidence level fusion with 145 ms of overhead. What is the modeled end to end latency?
variants.hint: Encoders run side by side, so only one of them sets the encoder term.
variants.explanation: The encoder term is the slowest admitted modality, so the estimate is 180 plus 310 plus 145, or 635 ms.

mistakes.feedback: Added the text and image encoder times together instead of taking the slower one.
Left out the task base latency.

variants.title: Budget the route
variants.context: The routing lab models a request as the task base latency plus the slowest admitted modality encoder plus the fusion overhead. Encoders run in parallel, so admitting a second cheap modality does not add its latency, and each fusion pattern carries its own overhead.
variants.prompt: The safety inspection task has a base latency of 260 ms. It admits image evidence at 310 ms and temporal frames at 760 ms, and it uses joint token fusion with 220 ms of overhead. What is the modeled end to end latency?
variants.hint: One admitted modality dominates the encoder term here.
variants.explanation: Temporal frames are the slowest admitted encoder, so the estimate is 260 plus 760 plus 220, or 1240 ms, which is why this route usually belongs in an asynchronous job.

mistakes.feedback: Summed the image and temporal encoder times instead of taking the slower one.
Left out the joint fusion overhead.

variants.title: Budget the route
variants.context: The routing lab models a request as the task base latency plus the slowest admitted modality encoder plus the fusion overhead. Encoders run in parallel, so admitting a second cheap modality does not add its latency, and each fusion pattern carries its own overhead.
variants.prompt: A team moves the meeting task from a cheap first cascade to joint token fusion. The base latency is 130 ms, it admits text at 35 ms and audio at 420 ms, and joint token fusion adds 220 ms of overhead. What is the modeled end to end latency?
variants.hint: Changing the fusion pattern changes only one term of the estimate.
variants.explanation: The audio encoder sets the encoder term, so the estimate is 130 plus 420 plus 220, or 770 ms; the fusion choice moved the overhead, not the encoding.

mistakes.feedback: Added the text encoder time on top of the audio encoder time.
Kept the 85 ms cascade overhead instead of the joint fusion overhead.

variants.title: Return the right response state
variants.context: A multimodal response has states, not just content. Completed, partial, needs review, rejected, and failed mean different things, and a fallback route must name the modality that was absent or degraded rather than implying that the missing evidence was verified.
variants.prompt: A compliance video review completes, but 12 percent of the intervals were unreadable. What should the response be?
options: A failed result, since the recording did not decode cleanly end to end.
A partial result with the interval map and the unreadable segments routed to review.
A completed result, since every readable interval was analyzed correctly.
optionFeedback: Most of the review succeeded, so discarding it wastes work the reviewer still needs.
Correct: the answer is usable but its coverage limit has to travel with it.
Completed would imply the whole recording was reviewed, which is exactly the false assurance to avoid.
variants.hint: Does the caller need the work, the limits, or neither?
variants.explanation: Partial plus a coverage report keeps the useful answer while preventing it from implying that unobserved evidence was checked.

variants.title: Return the right response state
variants.context: A multimodal response has states, not just content. Completed, partial, needs review, rejected, and failed mean different things, and a fallback route must name the modality that was absent or degraded rather than implying that the missing evidence was verified.
variants.prompt: The audio worker is unavailable, so a meeting summary can only use the agenda text. What should the API return?
options: A result that names audio as the absent modality and marks the summary degraded.
A completed summary built from the agenda, with no mention of the missing audio.
An empty response with no result and no explanation of the fallback.
optionFeedback: Correct: a fallback route must name the modality that was absent or degraded.
That implies decisions and owners were heard when nothing was transcribed.
The agenda based summary still has value, and silence hides which route ran.
variants.hint: What does the caller need in order to trust the fields it receives?
variants.explanation: A degraded route is only safe when the response names the missing modality, because the caller cannot otherwise tell which evidence backed the answer.

variants.title: Return the right response state
variants.context: A multimodal response has states, not just content. Completed, partial, needs review, rejected, and failed mean different things, and a fallback route must name the modality that was absent or degraded rather than implying that the missing evidence was verified.
variants.prompt: An upload exceeds the declared maximum duration for the task. What is the right control point?
options: Truncate the media silently and process the part that fits the limit.
Start decoding and stop when the deadline expires mid request.
Reject at admission with a stable error code before any decoding starts.
optionFeedback: Silent truncation produces claims about a recording the system never observed in full.
Unbounded decoding inside an open request is what the admission limit exists to prevent.
Correct: declared limits are enforced at the media boundary, before expensive work begins.
variants.hint: Which boundary is cheapest to fail at?
variants.explanation: Admission limits are published so callers can be rejected before work begins, which protects both the deadline and the truthfulness of coverage.

variants.title: Tell the modalities apart
variants.context: A modality is a distinct kind of evidence. Each one carries information the others cannot, needs its own preprocessing, and fails in its own way, which is why authority for a field must be assigned per task.
variants.prompt: Match each modality to the evidence it contributes that the others cannot.

pairs.label: Text and metadata
pairs.detail: Instructions, identifiers, retrieved context, and typed records in compact form.

pairs.label: Images
pairs.detail: Layout, handwriting, charts, color, and spatial relationships between objects.

pairs.label: Audio
pairs.detail: Speech, timing, speaker turns, and non verbal sound events.

pairs.label: Video
pairs.detail: Temporal order, so change and action across time become observable.

variants.hint: Ask what disappears from the task if that source is removed.
variants.explanation: A modality earns admission only when it supplies evidence another source cannot, since every admitted source costs latency, memory, and retention.

variants.title: Tell the modalities apart
variants.context: A modality is a distinct kind of evidence. Each one carries information the others cannot, needs its own preprocessing, and fails in its own way, which is why authority for a field must be assigned per task.
variants.prompt: Match each modality to the failure that its own preprocessing introduces.

pairs.label: Text extraction
pairs.detail: A transcript or field extraction can quietly omit detail the source still contains.

pairs.label: Image preprocessing
pairs.detail: Resizing or cropping can remove the exact region the task depends on.

pairs.label: Audio transcription
pairs.detail: Noise, overlap, and accent turn into confident but wrong words.

pairs.label: Video frame sampling
pairs.detail: A short decisive event can fall between two sampled frames.

variants.hint: Every one of these failures happens before the model sees anything.
variants.explanation: Preprocessing changes can regress a task with no model change, which is why crops, engines, and sampling policies are tested independently.

variants.title: Tell the modalities apart
variants.context: A modality is a distinct kind of evidence. Each one carries information the others cannot, needs its own preprocessing, and fails in its own way, which is why authority for a field must be assigned per task.
variants.prompt: Match each reported symptom to the stage that most likely produced it.

pairs.label: The total on the page is right, but the extracted field is off by one digit
pairs.detail: OCR extraction on the image, which should keep its region and confidence.

pairs.label: A named decision has no supporting words anywhere in the meeting
pairs.detail: Transcription coverage, where a segment produced no usable text.

pairs.label: An action visible in the recording is missing from the report
pairs.detail: Frame selection, which sampled past the interval that contained it.

pairs.label: The answer cites a record the user is not allowed to see
pairs.detail: Admission and policy, which should have filtered the source before fusion.

variants.hint: Trace back to the transformation, not to the model.
variants.explanation: Provenance through decoding, transcription, cropping, and sampling is what lets an operator name the stage that produced a wrong claim.
